analysis.one_liner: Bars data brokers from selling Americans' sensitive personal data to China, Russia, Iran, and North Korea.
analysis.headline: The House passed the bill 414 to 0, with no member voting no, but the Senate committee it was sent to never acted and the term ended without a Senate vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill makes it illegal for data brokers — companies that buy and resell personal information they did not collect directly from people — to sell sensitive data about people in the United States to China, Russia, Iran, or North Korea, or to companies those countries control. Covered data includes Social Security numbers, health information, bank account details, precise location history, private messages, biometric and genetic data, and more. The Federal Trade Commission would enforce the ban. The House passed it 414 to 0, but the Senate committee it was sent to never acted on it before the term ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Everyone living in the United States whose personal data is bought and sold. Data brokers could no longer sell Social Security numbers, health records, financial account details, precise location history, private messages, biometric and genetic data, and similar information to China, Russia, Iran, North Korea, or entities those countries control — a channel long used for spying, identity theft, and targeted scams against Americans [S5]. The FTC would enforce the ban [S5].
analysis.who_benefits_short: All Americans whose data is brokered

how_it_helps.text: It cuts off a documented espionage and fraud channel: data brokers would be barred from selling Social Security numbers, health and financial records, precise location history, private communications, biometric and genetic data, and data about members of the armed forces to China, Russia, Iran, North Korea, or entities at least 20 percent owned or controlled by those countries.
It covers the full range of brokers — any company that sells data it did not collect directly from the people it describes — rather than only a narrow list of firms.
It puts enforcement in the hands of the FTC using its existing unfair-and-deceptive-practices authority, so violations carry real penalties without creating a new bureaucracy.
It takes effect quickly, 60 days after enactment.

analysis.who_pays: Data brokers bear the cost: they could no longer sell Americans' sensitive data to China, Russia, Iran, North Korea, or companies they control, and would face FTC penalties for violations [S5]. Brokers would also bear the compliance cost of screening who they sell to. The bill creates no new agency funding; enforcement runs through the FTC's existing authorities [S5].
analysis.who_pays_short: Data brokers selling to adversary countries

drawbacks.text: The bill is narrow: it stops sales to four named adversary countries but leaves data brokers free to sell the same sensitive data to domestic buyers, to US-allied governments, and to anyone else, so it addresses a small slice of the data brokerage market.
It creates no right for individuals to sue and no opt-out; people whose data is sold still have no say, and protection depends entirely on FTC enforcement resources.
Large platforms and firms acting as 'service providers' are carved out, so much of the personal-data economy that actually holds Americans' information is untouched.
With such overwhelming bipartisan support in the House, its failure to get any Senate action suggests it was never prioritized by Senate leadership despite having the votes to likely pass.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The protection is real but modest: it closes a specific national-security and fraud channel used against Americans at almost no cost to the public, and the compliance burden falls only on brokers selling to the four named adversaries. The honest criticism is that it leaves the core problem standing — the same Social Security numbers, health records, and location histories can still be bought and sold domestically and exported to nearly any other country — so it functions as a targeted fix rather than a privacy right for Americans. A bill with unanimous House support and little industry defense deserved a Senate vote and did not get one.

outcome.mechanism: The House passed it unanimously, but the Senate Commerce Committee it was sent to never brought it up, and the term ended without a Senate vote.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on March 5, 2024, and referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee.
The committee took it up unusually fast: a subcommittee was discharged, a markup was held on March 7, and the committee ordered it reported 50-0 on March 7, reporting it on March 11.

The House passed the bill 414-0 under a suspension-of-the-rules procedure (a fast-track vote requiring two-thirds), with 202 of 213 Democrats and 212 of 219 Republicans voting yes and no member voting no.
The Senate received the bill on March 21, 2024, and referred it to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation, which took no further action.
The 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, without the Senate ever voting on the bill.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Data brokers and the broader data resale economy are better off: the bill died without a Senate vote, so they kept the ability to sell the same sensitive data to buyers at home and in countries other than the four named adversaries. Americans gained no new protection from this bill.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Data brokers and the data resale industry

sides.party_line_note: There was no partisan opposition: the House committee reported it 50-0 and the full House passed it 414-0, with 202 of 213 Democrats and 212 of 219 Republicans voting yes and no one voting no.

industries.note: The bill would cut off one of their sales channels: reselling Americans' Social Security numbers, health data, location histories, and private messages to China, Russia, Iran, North Korea, and entities they control. Their interest in keeping that market open runs against the protection the bill offers ordinary people.

industries.industry: Large tech platforms and ad-tech firms
industries.note: The bill defines 'data broker' to exclude entities transmitting or processing data at a customer's direction, so large platforms and ad-tech firms acting as service providers are not covered and keep their existing role in the personal-data economy. The underlying market in Americans' sensitive data continues.
